intro: People all over the world belong to religions. Your classmates, neighbors and friends may keep many different holidays. Some may follow no religion at all. In this unit you will learn how to study religion the way a fair scholar does.

First you will learn three parts most religions have: beliefs, practices and communities. You will learn what five symbols mean to the people who use them. Then you will fill a whole year with holidays. You will find out why some move and some stay put.
By the end, you will be able to describe a religion without judging it. You will use words like belief, tradition and sacred. And you will know when to say "Happy Diwali" or "Eid Mubarak."
bigQuestion: How can we learn about the beliefs and holidays of others in a fair and kind way?

write.prompt: Choose two holidays from this unit from two different religions. Using one text from the unit, such as Exodus 12:14, Luke 2:11 or Qur'an 2:185, explain what each holiday remembers, what people do, and why its date moves or stays.

Start with "Many Christians believe" or "Many Muslims believe."
Compare the two holidays; do not say one is better.
Use unit words like lunar, solar and commemorate.

title: What Is a Religion?

chapters.title: Beliefs, Practices, Communities
chapters.bigQuestion: How can we learn about a religion in a fair way, even if it is not our own?

story.title: Five Symbols on One Poster
story.kicker: A class makes a poster of five symbols and asks what each one means to the people who use it.
paragraphs: Ms. Reyes taped a big white poster to the wall. She drew five empty boxes on it. "Each group gets one symbol," she said. "Your job is to find out what it means to the people who use it." The class leaned in to see the cards she held up.

Omar's group got a cross. Priya's group got the word om, written in an old Indian script. Leo's group got a six-pointed star. Ana's group got a wheel with eight spokes. Jaspreet's group got a symbol with a sword in the middle, a circle and two curved swords.

The groups read library books. Some students asked family members. Omar said, "Christians use the cross to remember Jesus." Jaspreet said, "The khanda is a Sikh symbol. My grandpa has it on his car." Ana said her book called the wheel a sign of the Buddha's teaching.

Then Leo raised his hand. "What if a symbol means nothing to me?" he asked. Ms. Reyes smiled. "That is fine. You do not have to believe it. Our job is to learn what it means to others, and to say it fairly."

By Friday the poster was full. Each box had a symbol, a name and one sentence. Every sentence started the same way: "People who use this symbol believe..." The class read the poster out loud together.
story.think: Why did every sentence on the poster start with "People who use this symbol believe..."?

lessons.title: What People Believe
lessons.mainIdea: Most religions teach beliefs, ideas their followers hold to be true about life and what matters most.
reading: Many religions answer big questions. Where did the world come from? How should people treat each other? What happens after we die? The answers a religion teaches are its *beliefs*. Followers hold these ideas to be true.

Beliefs are different in each religion. Jews, Christians and Muslims believe in one God. Many Hindus worship many gods and goddesses. Many Hindus also see them as forms of one great spirit. Many Buddhists focus on the Buddha's teaching more than on a god.

People inside one religion do not always agree, either. Two Christians may believe some things differently. That is why we say "many Christians believe" and not "all Christians believe." Careful words help us be fair.

words.d: an idea a person holds to be true, such as an idea about God or about how to live
a way of life shared by a group, with beliefs, practices and a community

look.title: One God in the Torah
look.text: Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD.
look.prompt: Jews say a prayer called the Shema that begins with this line. What belief does it share?

check.q: What is a belief?
choices: An idea a person holds to be true
A holiday that comes once a year
A picture that stands for a group
check.why: A belief is an idea a person holds to be true. A building, holiday or picture is something else.

check.q: Which sentence talks about a religion in a fair way?
choices: Hindus are wrong about the gods.
Many Hindus believe there is one great spirit.
All Hindus believe exactly the same thing.
Everyone should believe what Hindus believe.
check.why: "Many Hindus believe" tells what followers hold without judging, and it does not claim everyone agrees.

check.q: Which three religions teach belief in one God?
check.why: Jews, Christians and Muslims all believe in one God. Buddhism does not center on a god.

lessons.title: What People Do
lessons.mainIdea: Religions are also practices, things followers do, like praying, eating special foods and keeping holidays.
reading: A religion is not only ideas. It is also things people do. Praying, singing, fasting and sharing food are *practices*. Practices are actions people repeat, often in the same way each time.

Many Muslims pray five times a day. Many Jewish families light candles on Friday night for Shabbat, the day of rest. Many Hindus do *puja* at home. Puja is worship with flowers, light and food offered to a god.
Some practices happen every day. Some happen once a year, like a holiday. Some happen once in a life, like a wedding. Watching what people do teaches a lot about what they believe.

words.d: something people do again and again as part of their religion, such as praying or fasting
Hindu worship, often with flowers, light and food offered to a god

look.title: A Friday Evening
look.text: It is Friday at sunset. A Jewish family lights two candles. They say a blessing over bread called challah. Next door, a Muslim family is back from Friday prayer at the mosque. Down the street, a Hindu grandmother offers a flower at a small shrine.
look.prompt: Name one practice in each home. Is each one done every day, every week or once a year?

check.q: What is a practice?
choices: An idea people hold to be true
Something people do again and again as part of their religion
check.why: A practice is an action, like praying or fasting. An idea held true is a belief.

check.q: What is puja?
choices: Hindu worship with flowers, light and food offered to a god
check.why: Puja is a Hindu practice. The Jewish day of rest is Shabbat.

check.q: Many Jewish families light candles on Friday night. What day are they starting?
check.why: Shabbat begins at sunset on Friday. Ramadan is Muslim, Diwali is Hindu and Easter is Christian.

lessons.title: Who They Do It With
lessons.mainIdea: Religions are communities, groups of people who gather and help each other, often at a house of worship.
reading: Most religions are shared. People pray together, eat together and help each other. A group like this is a *community*. A community can be a small family or millions of people around the world.
Many communities meet in a *house of worship*. Christians gather in churches. Jews gather in synagogues. Muslims gather in mosques. Hindus and Buddhists visit temples. Sikhs gather in a gurdwara.
Chicago has houses of worship of every kind. A church, a mosque and a temple may stand on the same street. Each one is a place where a community meets.

words.d: a group of people who share something and gather together
a building where a religious community gathers to pray or worship
a Sikh house of worship

look.title: Match the Place
look.text: A class makes cards: church, synagogue, mosque, temple, gurdwara. Then they make five more cards: Christians, Jews, Muslims, Hindus and Buddhists, Sikhs.
look.prompt: Match each group to its house of worship. Which card fits two groups?

check.q: What is a community?
choices: A group of people who share something and gather together
check.why: A community is a group. Religions are often shared by communities.

check.q: Where do Sikhs gather?
check.why: The gurdwara is the Sikh house of worship. Synagogues are Jewish, mosques are Muslim and churches are Christian.

check.q: Which pair is matched correctly?
check.why: Muslims gather in a mosque. The other pairs mix up the houses of worship.

lessons.title: The Cross and the Star
lessons.mainIdea: A symbol is a picture that stands for an idea; the cross stands for Christianity and the six-pointed star for Judaism.
reading: A *symbol* is a picture that stands for something bigger. A red heart can stand for love. Religions use symbols too. A symbol can help people remember what they believe.

The cross is the best-known symbol of Christianity. Christians believe Jesus died on a cross. They also believe God raised him to life. So for Christians, the cross stands for his death and for hope. Many churches have a cross.

The *Star of David* has six points. It is made of two triangles. It is a well-known symbol of Judaism. It is named for King David of the Hebrew Bible. You can see it on synagogues and on the flag of Israel.

words.d: a picture or object that stands for a bigger idea
a six-pointed star made of two triangles; a symbol of Judaism

look.title: Symbols All Around
look.text: Look at a stop sign, a flag and a heart on a card. None of them is the thing it stands for. A stop sign is not a rule, but it reminds us of one. A flag is cloth, but it stands for a country.
look.prompt: Why might a religion use a symbol instead of only words?

check.q: What is a symbol?
choices: A picture or object that stands for a bigger idea
A holiday that moves each year
check.why: A symbol stands for something bigger, like a heart for love.

check.q: Which religion uses the six-pointed Star of David?
check.why: The Star of David is a symbol of Judaism. The cross is a Christian symbol.

check.q: What do Christians believe the cross reminds them of?
choices: The day of rest on Friday night
That Jesus died and, they believe, was raised to life
check.why: Christians believe Jesus died on a cross and was raised. The other choices belong to other traditions.

lessons.title: The Crescent and the Khanda
lessons.mainIdea: The crescent moon and star is often linked to Islam, and the khanda is the symbol of the Sikhs.
reading: A thin, curved moon is called a *crescent*. A crescent with a star is often linked to Islam. You may see it on flags of some Muslim countries. The Islamic calendar follows the moon, so the moon matters to many Muslims.
Not every Muslim uses this symbol. Some Muslims say Islam has no official symbol at all. This is an example of people in one religion seeing things differently.

The *khanda* is the symbol of the Sikhs. It has a double-edged sword in the middle. A circle goes around it. Two curved swords sit on the sides. Many Sikhs say the symbol stands for one God and for standing up for what is right. You will often see it on a gurdwara's flag.

words.d: a thin, curved shape of the moon; with a star, often linked to Islam
the Sikh symbol, with a double-edged sword, a circle and two curved swords

look.title: Two Friends Disagree
look.text: Sara is Muslim. She says the crescent and star is a sign of Islam. Her cousin Yusuf is Muslim too. He says Islam has no official symbol, and the crescent is only a custom.
look.prompt: Can both cousins be Muslim and still see this differently? What does that teach about studying a religion?

check.q: Which symbol is the Sikh symbol?
check.why: The khanda, with swords and a circle, is the Sikh symbol.

check.q: Why does the moon matter to many Muslims?
choices: The Qur'an is written on the moon
The Islamic calendar follows the moon
check.why: The Islamic calendar is based on the moon, so moon shapes matter for dates.

check.q: Some Muslims say Islam has no official symbol. What does this show?
choices: Muslims do not have any beliefs
The crescent is a Christian symbol
People in one religion can see things differently
check.why: Different views inside one tradition are normal. That is why we say "many" or "some" Muslims.

lessons.title: Om and the Wheel
lessons.mainIdea: Om is a sacred sound for Hindus, and the eight-spoked wheel stands for the Buddha's teaching.
reading: *Om* is a sound and a symbol. Many Hindus say it at the start of prayers. They see it as a sacred sound. It is written in an old Indian script. Buddhists and Jains also use om in some chants.
The *dharma wheel* has eight spokes. It is a symbol of Buddhism. Dharma here means the Buddha's teaching. Buddhists say the Buddha set the wheel of teaching turning.
The eight spokes stand for the Eightfold Path. That is the Buddha's list of eight ways to live well. It includes right speech and right action. Many Buddhist temples show the wheel.

words.d: a sound many Hindus treat as sacred and say at the start of prayers
a wheel with eight spokes; a symbol of the Buddha's teaching

look.title: A Line from the Dhammapada
look.text: All that we are is the result of what we have thought.
look.cite: Dhammapada, verse 1, trans. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 10 (1881)
look.prompt: The Dhammapada is a Buddhist book of sayings. What does this line say about our thoughts?

check.q: What do the eight spokes on the dharma wheel stand for?
check.why: Buddhists link the eight spokes to the Eightfold Path of the Buddha's teaching.

check.q: Which religion most often uses om at the start of prayers?
check.why: Many Hindus begin prayers with om. Buddhists and Jains use it too, in some chants.

check.q: In the words "dharma wheel," what does dharma mean?
check.why: In Buddhism, dharma means the Buddha's teaching.

lessons.title: Tradition and Sacred
lessons.mainIdea: A tradition is what is handed down, and sacred means very special and set apart for holy use.
reading: A *tradition* is something handed down from older people to younger people. A family recipe can be a tradition. A religion is a tradition, too. Parents teach children the prayers, stories and holidays.

*Sacred* means very special, set apart for holy use. A sacred book is not treated like a comic book. Many people keep it high and handle it with care. A sacred place is one where people act with respect.
Different religions call different things sacred. For Muslims, the Qur'an is sacred. For Sikhs, the Guru Granth Sahib is sacred. For many Hindus, the Ganges River is sacred.

words.d: beliefs and customs handed down from older people to younger people
very special and set apart for holy use

look.title: Handed Down
look.text: Maya's grandma lights a lamp every Diwali. Her grandma did it too. Now Maya holds the match while Grandma watches. Next year, Maya will light it herself.
look.prompt: What makes this a tradition? Who will Maya hand it down to someday?

check.q: What does sacred mean?
choices: Very special and set apart for holy use
check.why: Sacred things are treated as holy and special, like a sacred book kept high.

check.q: Which is an example of a tradition?
choices: A prayer parents teach their children
check.why: A tradition is handed down, like a prayer passed from parents to children.

check.q: For many Hindus, which place is sacred?
check.why: Many Hindus treat the Ganges as sacred. Mecca is sacred to Muslims.

lessons.title: People of No Religion
lessons.mainIdea: Many people follow no religion, and they are part of every fair study of how people live.
reading: Not everyone follows a religion. Some people do not believe in God. They may be called *atheists*. Some people are not sure. They may be called *agnostic*. Many others just say "none."
People with no religion still ask big questions. They still care about being kind and fair. Many find meaning in family, nature, science or helping others.
Around the world, over a billion people follow no religion. That is about one in six people. In a fair class, their views count too. No one has to pick a religion.

words.d: a person who does not believe in God or gods
a person who is not sure whether God exists

look.title: People and Religion Around the World
look.cite: Common estimates for 2010, Pew Research Center (2012), rounded
look.prompt: Which group is the largest? Where does "no religion" come on the list?

check.q: What is an atheist?
choices: A person who is not sure
A person who does not believe in God or gods
A person who fasts in Ramadan
check.why: An atheist does not believe in God. A person who is not sure may be called agnostic.

check.q: About how many people in the world follow no religion?
check.why: Common estimates say over a billion people, about one in six, follow no religion.

check.q: Which sentence fits a fair class?
choices: People with no religion cannot be kind.
Only one religion should be studied.
No one has to pick a religion.
check.why: In a public school, students of any religion or none are welcome.

lessons.title: Describe, Do Not Judge
lessons.mainIdea: At school we learn about religions by describing them fairly, which is different from being part of one.
reading: Learning *about* a religion is not the same as joining it. A student can learn how Muslims pray without praying. A student can learn Christmas stories without being Christian. At school, we study. We do not practice.

The main rule is to *describe*, not judge. To describe is to tell what people believe and do. To judge is to say they are right or wrong. We say "Sikhs believe..." We do not say "Sikhs are right" or "Sikhs are wrong."
Good questions help. Ask, "What does this mean to you?" Do not tease about food, clothes or holidays. Every student should feel safe and welcome in class.

words.d: to tell what something is like without saying it is good or bad
to say whether something is right or wrong, good or bad

look.title: The Freedom to Choose
look.text: The government may not set up an official religion. It may not stop people from practicing their religion.
look.cite: First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution (1791), plain-words version
look.prompt: What two promises does this give? How do they help a class study religion fairly?

check.q: Which sentence describes and does not judge?
choices: Many Buddhists meditate to calm the mind.
Meditation is a silly thing to do.
Buddhists are wrong about the Buddha.
check.why: It tells what many Buddhists do without calling it good or bad.

check.q: How is learning about a religion different from being part of one?
choices: There is no difference at all
Learning about it means studying it, not practicing it
Learning about it means you must join
Being part of one means you cannot learn
check.why: At school students study what people believe and do; they are not asked to practice it.

check.q: A classmate brings a lunch you have never seen. What is a kind thing to do?
choices: Tell others not to sit near them
Ask, "What is it called?" in a friendly way
check.why: Asking kindly is a good question. Teasing about food makes people feel unsafe.

review.q: What are the three parts most religions have?
review.why: Most religions have what people believe, what they do and who they do it with.

review.q: Lighting Shabbat candles every Friday is an example of what?
review.why: A practice is something people do again and again, like lighting Shabbat candles.
The eight-spoked dharma wheel stands for the Buddha's teaching.

review.q: Which symbol is linked to Christianity?
review.why: Christians use the cross to remember Jesus's death and, they believe, his rising.

review.q: Where do Jews gather to pray?
review.why: The synagogue is the Jewish house of worship.

review.q: Which word means very special and set apart for holy use?
review.why: Sacred means set apart as holy.

review.q: Which sentence follows the class rule "describe, do not judge"?
review.why: It says what many Sikhs do without calling it good or bad.

review.q: A student says, "I do not follow any religion." What is true?
choices: They must pick one before class
Their view counts too in a fair class
They should leave during this unit
review.why: Over a billion people follow no religion. A fair class includes them.

chapters.title: A Year of Holidays
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do religions keep holidays, and why do some holidays move around the calendar?

story.title: Twelve Months on One Wall
story.kicker: A class puts a sticker on the calendar for every holiday it can name, and finds a puzzle.
paragraphs: Mr. Kim hung twelve pages on the long wall, one for each month. He passed out a sheet of star stickers. "Put a star on every holiday you know," he said. "Then write its name and who keeps it."

Stars went up fast. Grace put one on December 25 for Christmas. Arjun put one in the fall for Diwali. Mei put one in late January for Lunar New Year. Daniel put one in September for Rosh Hashanah. Aisha put one in March for Eid al-Fitr.

Then Aisha frowned. "Last year Eid was in April," she said. "And when my mom was little, it was in the winter." Daniel nodded. "Rosh Hashanah moves too, but not that much." Grace said, "Christmas never moves."
Mr. Kim wrote a question on the board: Why do some holidays move? "The answer is up in the sky," he said. "Some calendars follow the sun. Some follow the moon. Some follow both."
The class looked out the window at the pale moon in the morning sky. That week, they would learn what each holiday remembers, and why its star lands where it does.
story.think: Aisha remembers Eid in March, April and winter. What might make a holiday move like that?

lessons.title: Two Clocks in the Sky
lessons.mainIdea: Some calendars count years by the sun and some count months by the moon, and a few use both.
reading: People have always watched the sky to count time. Earth goes around the sun once a year. That takes about 365 days. A calendar that follows this trip is a *solar calendar*. The calendar on most school walls is solar.

The moon changes shape as it goes around Earth. It goes from new, to full, and back to new in about 29 and a half days. That is about one month. A calendar that counts moon months is a *lunar calendar*.

Twelve moon months add up to about 354 days. That is about 11 days shorter than a sun year. Some calendars add an extra month now and then to catch up with the sun. These use both the moon and the sun.

words.d: a calendar that follows the sun; a year is about 365 days
a calendar that counts months by the moon; a year is about 354 days

look.title: Counting a Year
look.prompt: How many days shorter is a year of twelve moon months than a sun year?

check.q: What does a solar calendar follow?
check.why: Solar means of the sun. A solar year is about 365 days.

check.q: About how long is one moon month?
check.why: The moon goes from new to full and back in about 29 and a half days.

check.q: Twelve moon months are shorter than a sun year by about how much?
check.why: 365 minus 354 is 11. That gap is why lunar dates move.

lessons.title: Why Some Holidays Move
lessons.mainIdea: Holidays set by the moon move on the school calendar, while Christmas stays on one date.
reading: The Islamic calendar is *lunar*. Each year its months start about 11 days earlier on the school calendar. So Ramadan, the month of fasting, moves. Over about 33 years, it passes through every season.

Easter moves too. In many churches, Easter is the first Sunday after the first full moon of spring. So it can fall in March or April. Many Orthodox Christians use an older calendar. Their Easter is often a little later.
Christmas does not move on the school calendar. Many Christians keep it on December 25 each year. Many Orthodox Christians keep it on January 7. That date matches December 25 on their older calendar.

words.d: the Muslim month of fasting, set by the moon
the Christian holiday of Jesus's rising, set by the spring full moon

look.title: Aisha's Puzzle
look.text: Aisha says Eid was in April last year and March this year. Her mom says it was in winter when she was a girl. Grace says Christmas is always on December 25.
look.prompt: Use the words lunar and solar to explain why Eid moves and Christmas does not.

check.q: Why does Ramadan move on the school calendar?
choices: Muslims pick a new date by vote
It follows a lunar calendar that is about 11 days shorter
It is set by the spring equinox only
check.why: The Islamic calendar is lunar, so Ramadan starts about 11 days earlier each year.

check.q: How do many churches set the date of Easter?
choices: The first Sunday after the first full moon of spring
check.why: Easter depends on the spring full moon, so it moves between March and April.

check.q: Many Orthodox Christians keep Christmas on which date?
check.why: January 7 on the school calendar matches December 25 on the older calendar many Orthodox churches use.

lessons.title: Lunar New Year
lessons.mainIdea: Lunar New Year starts on a new moon in late January or February and is kept by many families in East Asia and beyond.
reading: *Lunar New Year* is a big holiday in China, Korea, Vietnam and many other places. It is set by a calendar that uses the moon and the sun. It starts on a new moon between late January and mid February.

Families clean the house to sweep out the old year. They share big meals. Children may get red envelopes with money for good luck. Many people visit older relatives and honor their *ancestors*, family members who lived long ago.
In Chicago, Chinatown holds a parade with lion and dragon dancers. The holiday is not tied to only one religion. Families of many beliefs keep it, and some keep it with no religion at all.

words.d: a new-year holiday set by a moon-and-sun calendar, kept in China, Korea, Vietnam and beyond
a family member who lived long ago, such as a great-great-grandparent

look.title: Red Envelopes
look.text: Mei's grandma hands her a red envelope. "For a good year," she says. The table has dumplings and oranges. Before eating, the family bows toward photos of Mei's great-grandparents.
look.prompt: Which two customs show hope for the new year? Which one shows honor for ancestors?

check.q: When does Lunar New Year start?
choices: On a new moon in late January or February
On the first full moon of spring
check.why: Lunar New Year begins on a new moon between late January and mid February.

check.q: What is an ancestor?
choices: A new baby in the family
A family member who lived long ago
check.why: Ancestors are family from long ago. Many families honor them at Lunar New Year.

check.q: Which is a Lunar New Year custom?
choices: Fasting from sunrise to sunset for a month
check.why: Red envelopes are a Lunar New Year custom. Colored powder belongs to Holi.

lessons.title: A New Year in the Fall
lessons.mainIdea: Rosh Hashanah is the Jewish New Year, and ten days later comes Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement.
reading: The Jewish calendar uses the moon and the sun. Its new year comes in the fall. It is called *Rosh Hashanah*. That means "head of the year" in Hebrew. People hear the *shofar*, a horn made from a ram's horn.
Many families dip apples in honey. It is a wish for a sweet new year. Rosh Hashanah is also a time to think about the past year and how to do better in the year ahead.
Ten days later comes Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement. Many Jewish adults fast for about 25 hours. They pray in the synagogue. They ask God and other people for forgiveness.

words.d: the Jewish New Year in the fall; its name means "head of the year"
a horn made from a ram's horn, blown on Rosh Hashanah
the Jewish Day of Atonement, a day of fasting and asking forgiveness

look.title: The Blowing of Trumpets
look.text: In the seventh month, in the first day of the month, shall ye have a sabbath, a memorial of blowing of trumpets, an holy convocation.
look.prompt: Jews link Rosh Hashanah to this verse. What sound does it describe?

lessons.title: Passover
lessons.mainIdea: Passover remembers the story Jews tell of leaving slavery in Egypt, retold at a meal called the seder.
reading: In spring comes *Passover*. It remembers the story in the book of Exodus. Jews tell how God freed the Israelites from slavery in Egypt. Moses led them out.
Families share a special meal called a *seder*. They read the story aloud. Children ask four questions. The table has special foods. Bitter herbs remind them of the bitter times of slavery.
During Passover, many Jews eat *matzah*. It is flat bread with no yeast. The story says the Israelites left in such a hurry that their bread had no time to rise.

words.d: a Jewish spring holiday that remembers leaving slavery in Egypt
the Passover meal, where the Exodus story is read aloud
flat bread with no yeast, eaten at Passover

lessons.title: Christmas and Easter
lessons.mainIdea: Christians celebrate Jesus's birth at Christmas and, they believe, his rising from death at Easter.
reading: *Christmas* celebrates the birth of Jesus. The story is told in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke. Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God. Many go to church, sing carols and give gifts.

*Easter* is in the spring. Christians believe Jesus died on a cross and rose from death three days later. For many Christians, Easter is the most important day of the year. Churches fill with flowers and music.
The weeks before Easter are called Lent. Many Christians give something up during Lent. They pray more or give more to others. Customs are different in Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches.

words.d: the Christian holiday celebrating the birth of Jesus
the weeks before Easter, when many Christians pray more and give things up

check.why: Christmas celebrates Jesus's birth, told in Matthew and Luke.

check.why: Lent is the Christian time before Easter. Ramadan is the Muslim month of fasting.

lessons.title: Ramadan and Two Eids
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims fast in daylight during Ramadan, celebrate Eid al-Fitr at its end, and keep Eid al-Adha at the time of the pilgrimage.
reading: *Ramadan* is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar. Muslims believe the Qur'an was first sent down to the Prophet Muhammad in this month. Many adult Muslims fast from dawn to sunset. At sunset, families often break the fast with dates and water.
When the new moon ends Ramadan, *Eid al-Fitr* begins. Eid means feast. Families pray together, wear new clothes and visit friends. Many give food or money to people in need.

About two months later comes Eid al-Adha. It comes at the time of the Hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca. It remembers the Qur'an's story of Abraham's obedience to God. Many families share meat with neighbors and people in need.

words.d: the Muslim feast at the end of Ramadan
the Muslim feast at the time of the Hajj, remembering Abraham
to go without food and drink for a time, often as a religious practice

lessons.title: Diwali and Holi
lessons.mainIdea: Diwali is the Hindu festival of lights in the fall, and Holi is the spring festival of colors.
reading: *Diwali* is the festival of lights. It comes in October or November. Families light rows of small clay lamps called diyas. Many Hindus remember the story of Prince Rama coming home. Many also pray to Lakshmi, goddess of good fortune.
Diwali lasts about five days. People clean their homes, share sweets and wear new clothes. Sikhs and Jains also keep days of light at this time, each for their own reasons.
*Holi* comes in spring, often in March. People throw bright colored powder at each other. It celebrates spring and good winning over evil. Friends and strangers laugh together, all covered in color.

words.d: the Hindu festival of lights, in October or November
the Hindu spring festival of colors
a small clay oil lamp lit at Diwali

lessons.title: Vesak and Vaisakhi
lessons.mainIdea: Vesak honors the Buddha on a spring full moon, and Vaisakhi is a Sikh spring holiday remembering the Khalsa.
reading: *Vesak* is a Buddhist holiday on a full moon in April or May. Many Buddhists remember the Buddha's birth, his awakening and his death on this day. They bring flowers to temples. Many light lamps and give to people in need.
Some Buddhists keep these memories on separate days. Buddhists in Japan often mark the Buddha's birth on April 8. This shows how customs differ inside one tradition.

*Vaisakhi* is kept in April, usually on April 13 or 14. It is a harvest festival in Punjab, India. For Sikhs, it remembers 1699. That year Guru Gobind Singh started the *Khalsa*, the community of committed Sikhs. Many Sikhs march in parades and share free meals.

words.d: a Buddhist holiday on a spring full moon honoring the Buddha
a Sikh and Punjabi spring holiday in April
the community of committed Sikhs, begun by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699

check.why: Vesak honors the Buddha's birth, awakening and death on a full moon.

check.q: Who started the Khalsa?
check.why: Guru Gobind Singh was the tenth Sikh Guru.

lessons.title: A Year on One Wall
lessons.mainIdea: Putting holidays on one calendar shows what each one remembers and how different calendars work together.
reading: Look at a full year of holidays. Each one *commemorates* something. That means it remembers an event or honors a person. Passover remembers the Exodus. Christmas remembers Jesus's birth. Vesak remembers the Buddha.
Some holidays last one day. Others last about a week or even more. Ramadan lasts a whole month. The length is one way a tradition shows what matters most to it.
A shared calendar helps a school be fair. Teachers can plan tests so they do not land on big holidays. Friends can learn when to say "Happy Diwali" or "Eid Mubarak."

words.d: to remember an event or honor a person with a special day
a chart of the days, weeks and months of a year
